title: Acute limb ischaemia

header.contentArea: Applied surgical science and critical care

related.why: Compartment syndrome after reperfusion and fasciotomy

brief.scenario: Mrs Brenda Shaw, 78, developed sudden severe pain in her right leg 4 hours ago. She has atrial fibrillation; her warfarin was stopped after a fall last year. She has never had leg pain on walking. The right foot is pale and cold.
brief.task: The examiner will ask you about your assessment and management, giving findings as you ask.

beforeYouWalkIn.frame: Acutely ischaemic leg: grade it by sensation, movement and Doppler, heparinise, and get it revascularised on time.
beforeYouWalkIn.trap: Missing motor weakness, which turns a threatened limb into one that needs immediate surgery.
beforeYouWalkIn.firstMove: "ABCDE, then I'll examine both legs: pulses, sensation, movement and Doppler signals."

flow: Vascular specialist; imaging if no delay

grid.label: Embolus or thrombosis
grid.pass: Sudden onset with atrial fibrillation and no claudication suggests embolus; gradual worsening with claudication suggests thrombosis.
grid.high: Adds normal contralateral pulses favour embolus; plans to find and treat the embolic source.

grid.label: Examination and Rutherford grade
grid.fail: Checks pulses only, without sensation, movement or Doppler.
grid.pass: Tests sensation, movement and arterial and venous Doppler, and grades by Rutherford: I, IIa, IIb, III.
grid.high: Grades her IIb: sensory loss beyond the toes, weak dorsiflexion, arterial signal absent, venous present; salvageable with immediate revascularisation.

grid.label: Immediate treatment
grid.pass: IV unfractionated heparin; analgesia; oxygen; IV fluids; bloods including CK, U&E, clotting, group and save.
grid.high: Gives the dose: 5,000 IU (or 70–100 IU/kg) IV bolus, then infusion adjusted to APTT or ACT.

grid.label: Vascular referral and imaging
grid.pass: Urgent vascular specialist assessment now; CT angiography first-line if it won't delay treatment.
grid.high: Knows imaging must not delay a IIb limb; transfers to a vascular centre if this hospital lacks one.

grid.label: Revascularisation by grade (safety-critical)
grid.fail: Offers IV thrombolysis, or thrombolysis that cannot start promptly, or waits until morning with a motor deficit.
grid.pass: IIb: immediate revascularisation, here Fogarty balloon embolectomy; completion angiography; III: primary amputation.
grid.high: Knows catheter-directed thrombolysis suits IIa, only if started promptly in IIb; IV thrombolysis is not recommended.

grid.label: Reperfusion: compartments and potassium
grid.fail: Thinks the job ends when the pulse returns.
grid.pass: Watches for compartment syndrome after reperfusion, with fasciotomy if it develops; checks potassium, CK and urine output.
grid.high: Gets an ECG and gas; gives IV calcium gluconate only if the ECG shows hyperkalaemic changes, and insulin–glucose for K 6.5 mmol/L or more; anticipates acidosis and myoglobin-related AKI.

grid.label: Consent and decision-making
grid.fail: Consents without explaining amputation risk or her wishes.
grid.pass: Assesses her capacity; discusses risks including limb loss and death and her wishes; records decisions.
grid.high: Involves the consultant and family, and discusses ceilings of care in a frail patient.

fail.speaker: candidate
fail.text: I'd feel for her foot pulses.

fail.speaker: examiner
fail.text: There are no pulses below the femoral.

fail.speaker: candidate
fail.text: I'd give her paracetamol and book a duplex scan.

fail.speaker: examiner
fail.text: She can't move her toes well.

fail.speaker: candidate
fail.text: Thrombolysis overnight, and the vascular team can see her in the morning.

fail.speaker: examiner
fail.text: After embolectomy her calf becomes tense and very painful.

fail.speaker: candidate
fail.text: That's expected post-op pain; more morphine.

fail.speaker: candidate
fail.text: I'd get her to sign the form for embolectomy.

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: Acute limb ischaemia. Sudden onset with AF and no claudication suggests an embolus rather than thrombosis.

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: Pulses in both legs, sensation, movement, and Doppler signals, arterial and venous. Then I'd grade it by Rutherford.

pass.speaker: examiner
pass.text: Numb to mid-foot, weak dorsiflexion, no arterial signal, venous signal present.

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: IV unfractionated heparin, analgesia, oxygen and IV fluids. Bloods including CK, U&E, clotting and group and save.

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: I'd ask for an urgent vascular assessment now. CT angiography, but only if it won't delay treatment.

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: IIb: she needs immediate revascularisation, here a Fogarty embolectomy with completion angiography. A grade III leg would need primary amputation.

pass.speaker: examiner
pass.text: After embolectomy her calf becomes tense and very painful.

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: Compartment syndrome after reperfusion: she needs fasciotomy. I'd also check her potassium, CK and urine output.

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: I'd check she has capacity, explain the risks, including losing the leg and death, check what she wants, and record the decisions.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: Acute limb ischaemia, most likely embolic: sudden onset, untreated AF, no claudication. If her left leg pulses are normal, that supports it. We'll need to find and treat the source.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: Compare both legs: pulses, then sensation, movement and hand-held Doppler, arterial and venous. That grades it.

high.speaker: examiner
high.text: Numb to mid-foot, weak dorsiflexion, no arterial signal, venous signal present.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: That's Rutherford IIb: sensory loss beyond the toes and motor weakness. Immediately threatened but salvageable with immediate revascularisation.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: Unfractionated heparin now: 5,000 units IV, then an infusion adjusted to APTT. Morphine, oxygen, fluids, and bloods including CK and potassium.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: Vascular registrar and consultant now. CT angiography only if it doesn't delay theatre; with motor loss, it mustn't.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: IIb: immediate Fogarty embolectomy with completion angiography. Catheter thrombolysis suits IIa; in IIb only if it can start promptly. No IV thrombolysis. Grade III would mean primary amputation.

high.speaker: examiner
high.text: After embolectomy her calf becomes tense and very painful.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: Reperfusion compartment syndrome: fasciotomy now. Reperfusion also releases potassium: ECG and gas now. IV calcium gluconate if the ECG shows hyperkalaemic changes, and insulin–glucose for K 6.5 or more. And fluids, with CK and urine output for myoglobin-related kidney injury.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: She's frail, so with the consultant and her family I'd discuss limb loss, death and her wishes, including ceilings of care, and document it.

failures.move: Delaying revascularisation, or choosing slow thrombolysis, in a leg with motor loss.
failures.consequence: Safety-critical: a IIb limb becomes irreversible (III) and needs amputation.

failures.move: Feeling for pulses without testing sensation, movement and Doppler signals.
failures.consequence: Safety-critical: motor loss is missed, so the limb is under-graded and treated too late.

failures.move: Calling a tense, painful calf after revascularisation 'post-op pain'.
failures.consequence: Safety-critical: reperfusion compartment syndrome kills the muscle the operation just saved.

failures.move: Waiting for the vascular team before giving heparin.
failures.consequence: The clot propagates while she waits.

recovery.when: You forgot to grade the leg
recovery.line: Let me grade it: sensation, movement and Doppler put her in Rutherford IIb.

recovery.when: You can't recall the heparin dose
recovery.line: IV unfractionated heparin per the trust protocol now; I'd check the dose with pharmacy but not delay it.

knowledge.fact: Rutherford: I viable; IIa marginally threatened (toes numb or none, no weakness); IIb immediately threatened (sensory loss beyond toes, weakness); III irreversible (anaesthesia, paralysis, no Doppler signals).
Heparin while awaiting revascularisation: UFH 5,000 IU or 70–100 IU/kg, then infusion. CT angiography first line if it won't delay treatment.
Sudden onset suggests embolism; about two thirds of emboli are associated with atrial fibrillation.
Severe hyperkalaemia is 6.5 mmol/L or more: insulin–glucose. IV calcium only if the ECG shows hyperkalaemic changes.

recall.think: Losing the leg, then reperfusion: compartment syndrome and hyperkalaemia.
recall.say: "Rutherford IIb: immediately threatened. Heparin now and immediate revascularisation."
do: IV heparin, analgesia, fluids; vascular team now
recall.trap: A pink-ish foot with a venous signal can still be IIb if she can't move her toes.
recall.finish: Embolectomy (or bypass or endovascular treatment for thrombosis); primary amputation if irreversible.

sources.name: ICBSE Guide to the intercollegiate MRCS examination
sources.supports: Station format: 9 minutes with 1 minute's reading; examiner-led questioning in applied knowledge stations

sources.name: Björck M, Earnshaw JJ, Acosta S, et al. European Society for Vascular Surgery (ESVS) 2020 Clinical Practice Guidelines on the Management of Acute Limb Ischaemia. Eur J Vasc Endovasc Surg 2020;59:173-218
sources.supports: Urgent clinical assessment by a vascular specialist (Rec 3); Rutherford classification recommended (Rec 4; table: I viable, no sensory or motor loss, arterial and venous Doppler audible; IIa marginally threatened, salvageable if promptly treated, minimal (toes) or no sensory loss, no motor loss, arterial Doppler inaudible, venous audible; IIb immediately threatened, salvageable with immediate revascularisation, sensory loss beyond the toes with rest pain, mild or moderate muscle weakness, arterial inaudible, venous audible; III irreversible, profound anaesthesia and paralysis (rigor), both inaudible, major tissue loss or permanent nerve damage inevitable); imaging if it does not delay treatment (Rec 5), CT angiography first line (Rec 6); heparin while awaiting revascularisation (Rec 9); text: unfractionated heparin initially 5,000 IU or 70-100 IU/kg, then infusion adjusted to ACT or APTT; oxygen (Rec 10); analgesia and IV rehydration (Rec 11); transfer to a vascular centre (Rec 13); completion angiography (Rec 18); no IV thrombolysis (Rec 22); catheter-directed thrombolysis an alternative to surgery in IIa (Rec 24), may be considered in IIb if started promptly (Rec 25); motor loss (IIb): urgent revascularisation mandatory; primary amputation for irreversible (III) ischaemia; sudden onset suggests embolism, gradual worsening thrombosis; about two thirds of emboli are associated with atrial fibrillation; Fogarty balloon embolectomy standard for embolic occlusion; fasciotomy needed in 39% of one embolectomy series

sources.name: Rutherford RB, Baker JD, Ernst C, et al. Recommended standards for reports dealing with lower extremity ischemia: revised version. J Vasc Surg 1997;26:517-38
sources.supports: Original source of the acute limb ischaemia categories I, IIa, IIb and III (the station uses the table as reproduced in ESVS 2020)

sources.name: UK Kidney Association Clinical Practice Guidelines: Treatment of Acute Hyperkalaemia in Adults (Alfonzo A, Harrison A, Baines R, et al.)
sources.version: Original July 2020; updated October 2023 and July 2026
sources.supports: Severe hyperkalaemia 6.5 mmol/L or more; 12-lead ECG if K 6.0 or more; IV calcium first when the ECG shows hyperkalaemic changes; insulin-glucose to shift potassium; insulin–glucose for severe hyperkalaemia (6.5 mmol/L or more)

sources.name: Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery (O'Connell, McCaskie, Sayers, eds)
sources.supports: Normal contralateral pulses favour embolism; compartment syndrome after reperfusion needing fasciotomy; reperfusion releases potassium and myoglobin (hyperkalaemia, acidosis, acute kidney injury)

partner.opening: Mrs Shaw has just arrived in ED. What do you think is going on, and how would you manage her?

reveals.finding: Pain came on suddenly while watching television. No previous claudication. Warfarin stopped 14 months ago.
Right: femoral present; popliteal, dorsalis pedis and posterior tibial absent. Left leg: all pulses present. ECG: atrial fibrillation, rate 96.
Reduced sensation to mid-foot; weak dorsiflexion of the toes; no arterial Doppler signal at the ankle; venous signal present; calf soft.
K 5.1 mmol/L, CK 1,850 U/L, creatinine 104 µmol/L, INR 1.0.
Two hours after embolectomy: foot pink with palpable pedal pulses; calf tense and exquisitely tender on passive toe stretch. K 6.7 mmol/L.

push.question: What features separate an embolus from a thrombosis?
push.expect: Embolus: sudden onset, AF or another source, no claudication, normal contralateral pulses. Thrombosis: gradual worsening on a background of claudication.

push.question: Grade her limb and justify it.
push.expect: Rutherford IIb: sensory loss beyond the toes, motor weakness, absent arterial signal, venous signal present.

push.question: Why not thrombolysis?
push.expect: It is slower; for IIb only if started promptly; embolectomy restores flow immediately; IV thrombolysis is not recommended.

curveballs.prompt: Her foot is mottled and fixed, calf rigid, no arterial or venous signals.
curveballs.safeAnswer: Rutherford III, irreversible: revascularisation is futile and dangerous; discuss primary amputation or palliation with the consultant and family.

curveballs.prompt: The radiographer can scan her in 90 minutes.
curveballs.safeAnswer: Imaging must not delay a IIb limb: she goes to theatre, with on-table angiography.

curveballs.prompt: A 70-year-old with years of calf claudication now has a cold IIa foot.
curveballs.safeAnswer: Likely thrombosis on existing disease: heparin, CT angiography to plan; bypass, endovascular treatment or catheter-directed thrombolysis.
